title: Hotel schema in PostgreSQL
idea: The hotel schema stores one inventory row per room type per night, so taking a stay is a locked, conditional update of exactly its nights.

analogy.text: A wall calendar per room type, with one square per night showing rooms sold out of rooms owned. A stay crosses out one unit in each of its squares.
analogy.breaks: Squares here are locked while written; a wall calendar is not.

points: `room_inventory` has key (room type, night) and a CHECK that reserved stays within total.
`reservation` maps the Java model: TEXT status with CHECK, BIGINT money, DATE stay.
An exclusion constraint stops two live stays sharing one physical room on any night.
Partial index on HELD rows by `hold_until` serves the expiry sweeper only.

hero.title: The update that takes a stay

parts.label: table
parts.note: One row per room type per night. The PRIMARY KEY is (room_type_id, night).

parts.label: take one
parts.note: Add one unit relative to the row's current value, never a value read earlier.

parts.label: which type
parts.note: The guest books a room type, so inventory is counted per type.

parts.label: half-open stay
parts.note: Check-in night included, check-out night excluded. Back-to-back stays never collide.

parts.label: guard
parts.note: A sold-out night is skipped, so fewer rows come back than nights asked.

parts.label: price
parts.note: Each night returns its own rate. Row count below nights means roll back.

code.title: Tables and constraints
code.caption: The schema on a real PostgreSQL 18, then five bad writes the database refuses by itself, and one valid back-to-back stay.

walk.text: Hotel, room type, room and guest. `btree_gist` lets an exclusion constraint compare TEXT ids.
`room_inventory`: one row per type and night, with a CHECK on reserved.
`reservation` keeps status as TEXT with CHECK, money as BIGINT, and a unique Idempotency-Key.
Same room, no overlapping live stays: `&&` means date ranges overlap; refusals fail with 23P01, an exclusion violation.
Partial index for the sweeper; a second index serves a guest's trip list.
Seed seven nights of Deluxe inventory, two rooms each, at one rate.
Each bad write prints the Postgres error code and the constraint that stopped it.

code.title: Hold and sweep transactions
code.caption: Two overlapping holds race for the last Deluxe room on the 14th; then the sweeper frees it. Trimmed tables keep it short.

walk.text: One Deluxe room per night from the 13th to the 16th.
Lock the stay's nights in date order with `FOR UPDATE`, so overlapping stays queue.
Take one unit from each night that still has room.
A missing or sold-out night means fewer rows: roll back everything.
Otherwise sum the nightly rates and insert a HELD reservation for 15 minutes.
Sweeper: expire due holds, then GROUP BY night so each inventory row joins once.
Two holds in parallel on separate connections; the locks decide one winner.

pitfalls: Do not use UPDATE ... FROM with duplicate join rows; Postgres updates each target once.
Lock nights in one fixed order, or two long stays can deadlock each other.
Keep a CHECK on reserved even with careful code; it catches every forgotten path.

quiz.q: What does reserve.mjs print for 'nights freed at 09:10'?
quiz.why: The winning hold lasts until 09:15. At 09:10 no HELD row is due, so the sweeper changes no inventory rows.

takeaway: One row per type per night turns overbooking into a failed conditional update.

starters: Why count inventory per night instead of searching overlapping reservations?
